### 2020

::: {.question-card #matrices-2020-mj-11-12}
### 2020 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 6 · 13 marks

Let

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** The transformation represented by $A^{-1}$ maps a triangle of area $30\text{ cm}^2$ to a triangle of area $d\text{ cm}^2$. Find $d$. **[3]**

**(b)** Prove by induction that, for every positive integer $n$,

$$
A^n=\begin{pmatrix}2^n&0\\2^n-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**[5]**

Let $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\33&0\end{pmatrix}$.

**(c)** The line $y=2x$ is invariant under the transformation represented by $A^nB$. Find $n$. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Since

$$
\det A=2,\qquad \det(A^{-1})=(\det A)^{-1}=\frac12,
$$

the area scale factor is $\left|\det(A^{-1})\right|=\frac12$. Therefore

$$
\boxed{d=30\times\frac12=15}.
$$

**(b)** For $n=1$,

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2^1&0\\2^1-1&1\end{pmatrix},
$$

so the statement is true initially. Assume that it is true for $n=k$, where $k$ is a positive integer:

$$
A^k=\begin{pmatrix}2^k&0\\2^k-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Then

$$
A^{k+1}=\begin{pmatrix}2^k&0\\2^k-1&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2^{k+1}&0\\2^{k+1}-1&1\end{pmatrix},
$$

Thus the statement is true for $k+1$ whenever it is true for $k$. Hence, by mathematical induction,

$$
\boxed{A^n=\begin{pmatrix}2^n&0\\2^n-1&1\end{pmatrix}}
$$

for every positive integer $n$.

**(c)** Using part (b),

$$
A^nB=\begin{pmatrix}2^n&0\\2^n+32&0\end{pmatrix}.
$$

For a general point $(x,y)$,

$$
A^nB\binom xy
=\binom{2^nx}{(2^n+32)x}.
$$

The image has gradient $(2^n+32)/2^n$. Since the invariant line has gradient $2$,

$$
\frac{2^n+32}{2^n}=2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
2^n=32
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{n=5}.
$$

</details>

<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2020, Q6; 9231/12/M/J/2020, Q6.</div>

::: {.question-card #matrices-2020-mj-13}
### 2020 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 4 · 11 marks

Let

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}k&0&2\\0&-1&-1\\1&1&-k\end{pmatrix},\quad
B=\begin{pmatrix}0&-3\\-1&3\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
C=\begin{pmatrix}-3&-1&1\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** Show that $A$ is non-singular. **[3]**

It is given that

$$
CAB=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-\frac32\\-1&-\frac32\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(b)** Find $k$. **[3]**

**(c)** Find the invariant lines through the origin of the transformation represented by $CAB$. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Expanding along the first row,

$$
\det A
=k\begin{vmatrix}-1&-1\\1&-k\end{vmatrix}
+2\begin{vmatrix}0&-1\\1&1\end{vmatrix}
=k(k+1)+2
=k^2+k+2.
$$

The discriminant of $k^2+k+2$ is

$$
1^2-4(1)(2)=-7<0.
$$

Since its leading coefficient is positive, $k^2+k+2>0$ for every real $k$. Thus $\det A\ne0$ and $A$ is non-singular.

**(b)** First,

$$
AB=\begin{pmatrix}0&-3k\\1&-3\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},
$$

and hence

$$
CAB
=\begin{pmatrix}-2&9k+3\\-1&-3k-3\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Comparing, for example, the top-right entry with the given matrix,

$$
9k+3=-\frac32
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{k=-\frac12}.
$$

**(c)** The given $CAB$ maps a point $(x,y)$ to

$$
\binom XY
=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-\frac32\\-1&-\frac32\end{pmatrix}
\binom xy
=\binom{-2x-\frac32y}{-x-\frac32y}.
$$

For the line $y=mx$, substitute $y=mx$ and require $Y=mX$:

$$
-1-\frac32m=m\left(-2-\frac32m\right),
$$

Thus

$$
3m^2+m-2=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
(3m-2)(m+1)=0.
$$

Therefore

$$
\boxed{y=\frac23x\quad\text{or}\quad y=-x}.
$$

</details>

### 2020 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 1 · 9 marks

Let

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}1&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
$$

where $a,b>0$.

**(a)** State the two transformations represented by $M$, in the correct order. **[2]**

The unit square is mapped by $M$ onto parallelogram $OPQR$.

**(b)** Find the matrix mapping $OPQR$ back onto the unit square. **[2]**

**(c)** Given that the area of $OPQR$ is $2\text{ cm}^2$ and $x+3y=0$ is invariant, find $a$ and $b$. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Reading the product from right to left, first apply a one-way stretch parallel to the $x$-axis with scale factor $a$, then a shear with the $x$-axis fixed, taking $(0,1)$ to $(b,1)$.

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}1&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(b)** Since $\det M=a$,

$$
\boxed{M^{-1}=\frac1a\begin{pmatrix}1&-b\\0&a\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(c)** The unit square has area $1$, so its image has area

$$
|\det M|=a.
$$

As $a>0$ and the given area is $2$, $\boxed{a=2}$. A general point on $x+3y=0$ can be written as $(x,-x/3)$. Its image is

$$
\binom XY
=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\binom{x}{-x/3}
=\binom{ax-\frac13bx}{-\frac13x}.
$$

The image must again satisfy $X+3Y=0$:

$$
ax-\frac13bx-x=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
1=a-\frac b3.
$$

Using $a=2$ gives $\boxed{b=3}$, so $\boxed{a=2, b=3}$.

</details>

### 2020 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 4 · 13 marks

Let

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{pmatrix}\frac12&-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\[2pt]\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&\frac12\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** Identify the transformation represented by $A$. **[1]**

**(b)** Identify the transformation represented by $B$. **[2]**

Triangle $DEF$ is transformed by $AB$ onto triangle $PQR$.

**(c)** Show that the two triangles have the same area. **[3]**

**(d)** Find the matrix mapping $PQR$ onto $DEF$. **[2]**

**(e)** Find the invariant lines through the origin of the transformation represented by $AB$. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** $A$ represents reflection in the line $y=x$.

**(b)** Comparing $B$ with the standard rotation matrix shows that it represents a rotation through $60^\circ$ anticlockwise about the origin.

**(c)** Multiplying in the stated order,

$$
AB=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&\frac12\\[2pt]\frac12&-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \det(AB)=-1,
$$

Therefore the area scale factor is $|\det(AB)|=1$, so triangles $DEF$ and $PQR$ have equal area.

**(d)** Using the $2\times2$ inverse formula,

$$
\boxed{(AB)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&\frac12\\[2pt]\frac12&-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(e)** Under $AB$,

$$
\binom XY
=\binom{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}x+\frac12y}{\frac12x-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}y}.
$$

Put $y=mx$ and require $Y=mX$:

$$
\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}m
=m\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac12m\right).
$$

Hence

$$
m^2+2\sqrt3m-1=0,
$$

so $m=-\sqrt3\pm2$. Therefore

$$
\boxed{y=(2-\sqrt3)x\quad\text{or}\quad y=-(2+\sqrt3)x}.
$$

{{< include figures/matrices/past-2020-on-12.svg >}}

</details>

### 2021

::: {.question-card #matrices-2021-mj-11-12}
### 2021 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 4 · 14 marks

A rotation of $60^\circ$ anticlockwise about the origin is followed by a one-way stretch in the $x$-direction with scale factor $d$, where $d\ne0$.

**(a)** Find the matrix $M$ of the combined transformation. **[4]**

**(b)** The unit square is mapped by $M$ onto a parallelogram of area $\frac12d^2$. Show that $d=2$. **[2]**

Let $N$ satisfy

$$
MN=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\[2pt]\frac12&\frac12\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(c)** Find $N$. **[3]**

**(d)** Find the invariant lines through the origin of the transformation represented by $MN$. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** The rotation matrix is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}\frac12&-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\[2pt]\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&\frac12\end{pmatrix},
$$

and the following stretch has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}d&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Hence, in the correct order,

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}d&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\frac12&-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\[2pt]\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&\frac12\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}\frac d2&-\frac{d\sqrt3}{2}\\[2pt]\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&\frac12\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(b)** Since

$$
\det M=\frac d4+\frac{3d}{4}=d,
$$

the image area is $|d|$. In the geometrical stretch context $d>0$, so

$$
d=\frac12d^2.
$$

As $d\ne0$, $\boxed{d=2}$.

**(c)** With $d=2$,

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}1&-\sqrt3\\[2pt]\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&\frac12\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
M^{-1}=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}\frac12&\sqrt3\\[2pt]-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Therefore

$$
N=M^{-1}(MN)
=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}\frac12&\sqrt3\\[2pt]-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\[2pt]\frac12&\frac12\end{pmatrix}
$$

and hence

$$
\boxed{N=\frac14\begin{pmatrix}1+\sqrt3&1+\sqrt3\\1-\sqrt3&1-\sqrt3\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(d)** Under $MN$,

$$
\binom XY
=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\[2pt]\frac12&\frac12\end{pmatrix}
\binom xy
=\binom{x+y}{\frac12x+\frac12y}.
$$

For $y=mx$, the condition $Y=mX$ gives

$$
\frac12+\frac12m=m(1+m)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
2m^2+m-1=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
(2m-1)(m+1)=0.
$$

Thus

$$
\boxed{y=\frac12x\quad\text{or}\quad y=-x}.
$$

</details>

### 2021 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 4 · 11 marks

Let

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}2&k&k\\5&-1&3\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
C=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&1\\-1&2&0\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** Find $CAB$. **[3]**

**(b)** Given that $A$ is singular, find $k$. **[3]**

**(c)** Using this value of $k$, find the invariant lines through the origin of the transformation represented by $CAB$. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** First,

$$
AB=\begin{pmatrix}2+k&k\\8&-1\\2&0\end{pmatrix},
$$

so

$$
CAB
=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&1\\-1&2&0\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}2+k&k\\8&-1\\2&0\end{pmatrix}
=\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}10&-1\\14-k&-k-2\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(b)** Expanding $\det A$ along the first row,

$$
\det A
=2\begin{vmatrix}-1&3\\0&1\end{vmatrix}
-k\begin{vmatrix}5&3\\1&1\end{vmatrix}
+k\begin{vmatrix}5&-1\\1&0\end{vmatrix}
=-2-k.
$$

Since $A$ is singular, $-2-k=0$, giving $\boxed{k=-2}$.

**(c)** Hence

$$
CAB=\begin{pmatrix}10&-1\\16&0\end{pmatrix},
$$

which maps $(x,mx)$ to $(10x-mx,16x)$. Requiring $Y=mX$ gives

$$
16=m(10-m),
$$

so $m^2-10m+16=0$. Therefore $\boxed{y=2x}$ or $\boxed{y=8x}$.

</details>

### 2021 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 4 · 11 marks

Let

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** State the two transformations represented by $M$, in the correct order. **[2]**

**(b)** For $0\le\theta\le\pi$, find the values of $\theta$ for which the transformation has exactly one invariant line through the origin. **[9]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Reading the product from right to left, first apply a one-way stretch parallel to the $x$-axis with scale factor $3$, then rotate anticlockwise through $\theta$ about the origin.

**(b)** Multiplying gives

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}3\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\3\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}.
$$

For a point $(x,mx)$,

$$
X=(3\cos\theta-m\sin\theta)x,
\qquad
Y=(3\sin\theta+m\cos\theta)x.
$$

Requiring $Y=mX$ gives

$$
3\sin\theta+m\cos\theta
=3m\cos\theta-m^2\sin\theta,
$$

which reduces to

$$
m^2\sin\theta-2m\cos\theta+3\sin\theta=0.
$$

Exactly one finite-gradient invariant line requires a repeated root, so the discriminant must be zero:

$$
4\cos^2\theta-12\sin^2\theta=0.
$$

Thus $\tan^2\theta=1/3$. In the stated interval this gives

$$
\boxed{\theta=\frac\pi6\text{ or }\frac{5\pi}6}.
$$

At the endpoints $\theta=0,\pi$, both coordinate axes are invariant, so neither endpoint satisfies “exactly one”.

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="matrices-2021-on-11-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2021, Q4; 9231/13/O/N/2021, Q4.</div>

::: {.question-card #matrices-2021-on-12}
### 2021 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 1 · 9 marks

**(a)** Describe the transformation represented by $\begin{pmatrix}6&0\\0&6\end{pmatrix}$. **[1]**

Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$.

**(b)** A triangle of area $13\text{ cm}^2$ is transformed by $A$. Find the area of its image. **[2]**

**(c)** Find $B$ such that $AB=\begin{pmatrix}6&0\\0&6\end{pmatrix}$. **[2]**

**(d)** Show that the origin is the only invariant point of the transformation represented by $A$. **[4]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** The matrix $6I$ represents an enlargement with centre the origin and scale factor $6$.

**(b)**

$$
\det A=3(2)-4(2)=-2.
$$

Hence the area scale factor is $|-2|=2$, and the image area is

$$
\boxed{2\times13=26\text{ cm}^2}.
$$

**(c)** Since $AB=6I$,

$$
B=A^{-1}(6I)=6A^{-1}.
$$

Now

$$
A^{-1}=-\frac12\begin{pmatrix}2&-4\\-2&3\end{pmatrix},
$$

so

$$
\boxed{B=6A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}-6&12\\6&-9\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(d)** If $(x,y)$ is invariant, then

$$
\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\2&2\end{pmatrix}\binom xy=\binom xy.
$$

Thus

$$
3x+4y=x,\qquad 2x+2y=y,
$$

or

$$
2x+4y=0,\qquad 2x+y=0.
$$

The second equation gives $y=-2x$; substituting into the first gives $-6x=0$. Hence $x=0$ and $y=0$, so the origin is the only invariant point.

</details>

### 2022

::: {.question-card #matrices-2022-mj-11-12}
### 2022 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 7 · 17 marks

Let

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&k&6\\7&8&9\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** Find the set of values of $k$ for which $A$ is non-singular. **[3]**

**(b)** Given that $A$ is non-singular, find the entries in the top row of $A^{-1}$. **[4]**

Let $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

**(c)** Give an example of a matrix $C$ such that

$$
BAC=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\k&4\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**[4]**

**(d)** Find the set of values of $k$ for which the transformation represented by $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\k&4\end{pmatrix}$ has two distinct invariant lines through the origin. **[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Expanding along the first row,

$$
\det A
=1\begin{vmatrix}k&6\\8&9\end{vmatrix}
-2\begin{vmatrix}4&6\\7&9\end{vmatrix}
+3\begin{vmatrix}4&k\\7&8\end{vmatrix}
$$

$$
=(9k-48)-2(36-42)+3(32-7k)
=60-12k.
$$

Thus $A$ is non-singular when

$$
\boxed{k\ne5}.
$$

**(b)** The top row of $A^{-1}=(\det A)^{-1}\operatorname{adj}A$ is formed from the cofactors of the first column:

$$
(A^{-1})_{11}=\frac{\begin{vmatrix}k&6\\8&9\end{vmatrix}}{60-12k}
=\frac{3k-16}{4(5-k)},
$$

$$
(A^{-1})_{12}=\frac{-\begin{vmatrix}2&3\\8&9\end{vmatrix}}{60-12k}
=\frac1{2(5-k)},
$$

$$
(A^{-1})_{13}=\frac{\begin{vmatrix}2&3\\k&6\end{vmatrix}}{60-12k}
=\frac{4-k}{4(5-k)}.
$$

Therefore the top row is

$$
\boxed{\left(\frac{3k-16}{4(5-k)},\ \frac1{2(5-k)},\ \frac{4-k}{4(5-k)}\right)}.
$$

**(c)** Since

$$
BA=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&k&6\end{pmatrix},
$$

one valid choice is

$$
\boxed{C=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

Indeed,

$$
BAC
=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&k&6\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\k&4\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(d)** Let $T=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\k&4\end{pmatrix}$. Then

$$
T\binom{x}{mx}=\binom{(2+m)x}{(k+4m)x}.
$$

For $y=mx$ to be invariant, $Y=mX$:

$$
k+4m=m(2+m),
$$

giving

$$
m^2-2m-k=0.
$$

Two distinct invariant lines require

$$
\Delta=(-2)^2-4(1)(-k)=4+4k>0,
$$

so $k>-1$. Also $T$ must be non-singular:

$$
\det T=8-k\ne0.
$$

Therefore

$$
\boxed{k>-1,\qquad k\ne8}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="matrices-2022-mj-11-12"> Completed</label>

::: {.question-card #matrices-2022-mj-13}
### 2022 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 5 · 12 marks

Let

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&a\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
$$

where $a>0$.

**(a)** State the type of transformation represented by $A$. **[1]**

**(b)** Prove by induction that

$$
A^n=\begin{pmatrix}1&na\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
$$

for every positive integer $n$. **[5]**

Let

$$
B=\begin{pmatrix}b&b\\1/a&1/a\end{pmatrix},
$$

where $b>0$.

**(c)** Find the invariant lines through the origin of the transformation represented by $A^nB$. **[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** $A$ represents a shear in the $x$-direction, with the $x$-axis fixed and $(0,1)$ mapped to $(a,1)$.

**(b)** For $n=1$, the stated formula is exactly the given matrix $A$. Assume that it holds for $n=k$:

$$
A^{k+1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&ka\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1&a\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&(k+1)a\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Therefore the statement holds for $k+1$ whenever it holds for $k$. Hence, by mathematical induction, it is true for every positive integer $n$.

**(c)** Using the result from part (b),

$$
A^nB=\begin{pmatrix}b+n&b+n\\1/a&1/a\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Thus

$$
\binom XY
=\binom{(b+n)(x+y)}{(x+y)/a}.
$$

For $y=mx$, require $Y=mX$:

$$
\frac{1+m}{a}=m(b+n)(1+m).
$$

Hence

$$
(1+m)\left\{\frac1a-m(b+n)\right\}=0,
$$

so

$$
\boxed{y=-x\quad\text{or}\quad y=\frac{x}{a(b+n)}}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="matrices-2022-mj-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2022, Q5.</div>

### 2023 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 5 · 15 marks

Let

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&k&3\\2&1&3\\3&2&5\end{pmatrix},\quad
B=\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\-1&3\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
C=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-1&1\\1&1&3\end{pmatrix}.
$$

It is given that $A$ is singular.

**(a)** Show that $CAB=\begin{pmatrix}3&-7\\-9&3\end{pmatrix}$. **[5]**

**(b)** Find the invariant lines through the origin of the transformation represented by $CAB$. **[5]**

Matrices $D,E,F$ represent, respectively, an enlargement centred at the origin, a stretch parallel to the $x$-axis, and reflection in $y=x$.

**(c)** Given that $CAB=D-9EF$, find $D,E,F$. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Since $A$ is singular,

$$
0=\det A
=1\begin{vmatrix}1&3\\2&5\end{vmatrix}
-k\begin{vmatrix}2&3\\3&5\end{vmatrix}
+3\begin{vmatrix}2&1\\3&2\end{vmatrix}
=-1-k+3.
$$

Thus $\boxed{k=2}$. Then

$$
AB
=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&1&3\\3&2&5\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\-1&3\\0&0\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-2&4\\-1&-1\\-2&0\end{pmatrix},
$$

and

$$
CAB
=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-1&1\\1&1&3\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}-2&4\\-1&-1\\-2&0\end{pmatrix}
=\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}3&-7\\-9&3\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(b)** This matrix maps $(x,y)$ to

$$
\binom XY=\binom{3x-7y}{-9x+3y}.
$$

For $y=mx$, require $Y=mX$:

$$
-9+3m=m(3-7m),
$$

so $7m^2=9$ and

$$
\boxed{y=\frac3{\sqrt7}x\quad\text{or}\quad y=-\frac3{\sqrt7}x}.
$$

**(c)** The stated geometrical descriptions give

$$
D=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&0\\0&\alpha\end{pmatrix},\qquad
E=\begin{pmatrix}\beta&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
F=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Therefore

$$
D-9EF
=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&0\\0&\alpha\end{pmatrix}
-9\begin{pmatrix}0&\beta\\1&0\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&-9\beta\\-9&\alpha\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Comparing this with $CAB=\begin{pmatrix}3&-7\\-9&3\end{pmatrix}$ gives $\alpha=3$ and $\beta=7/9$. Hence

$$
\boxed{D=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix},\quad
E=\begin{pmatrix}7/9&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
F=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

</details>

### 2023 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 3 · 8 marks

Let

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}k&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix},
$$

where $k\ne0,1$.

**(a)** State the two transformations represented by $M$, in the correct order. **[2]**

The unit square is transformed by $M$ onto parallelogram $OPQR$.

**(b)** Find its area and the matrix mapping $OPQR$ back onto the unit square. **[3]**

**(c)** Show that the line through the origin with gradient $1/(k-1)$ is invariant. **[3]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Reading from right to left, first apply a shear in the $y$-direction, with the $y$-axis fixed and $(1,0)$ mapped to $(1,1)$. Then apply a one-way stretch parallel to the $x$-axis with scale factor $k$.

**(b)** Multiplication gives

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}k&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix},
$$

The determinant is $k$, so the image of the unit square has area $\boxed{|k|}$ square units. Under the paper's geometrical scale-factor convention $k>0$, this is written as $\boxed{k}$ in the mark scheme.

Also,

$$
\boxed{M^{-1}=\frac1k\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-1&k\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(c)** A direction vector for the given line is

$$
\mathbf v=\binom{1}{1/(k-1)}.
$$

Then

$$
M\mathbf v=\binom{k}{k/(k-1)}=k\mathbf v,
$$

which proves invariance.

{{< include figures/matrices/past-2023-on-12.svg >}}

</details>

### 2024 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 4 · 13 marks

Let

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}\frac12&-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\[2pt]\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&\frac12\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}14&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** Give full details of the two transformations represented by $M$, in the correct order. **[4]**

**(b)** Write $M^{-1}$ as the product of two matrices, neither equal to $I$. **[2]**

**(c)** Find the invariant lines through the origin of the transformation represented by $M$. **[5]**

Triangle $ABC$ is transformed by $M$ onto triangle $DEF$ of area $28\text{ cm}^2$.

**(d)** Find the area of triangle $ABC$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Reading from right to left, first apply a one-way stretch parallel to the $x$-axis with scale factor $14$, then rotate anticlockwise through $\pi/3$ about the origin.

**(b)** Using $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$, reverse the order and invert each factor:

$$
\boxed{M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1/14&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\frac12&\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\[2pt]-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&\frac12\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

Since

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}7&-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\[2pt]7\sqrt3&\frac12\end{pmatrix},
$$

**(c)** A point $(x,mx)$ maps to

$$
X=7x-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}mx,
\qquad
Y=7\sqrt3x+\frac12mx.
$$

Requiring $Y=mX$ gives

$$
7\sqrt3+\frac12m
=7m-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}m^2,
$$

or

$$
\sqrt3m^2-13m+14\sqrt3=0.
$$

This factorises through the roots $m=2\sqrt3$ and $m=7\sqrt3/3$. Hence

$$
\boxed{y=2\sqrt3x\quad\text{or}\quad y=\frac{7\sqrt3}{3}x}.
$$

**(d)** Since determinants multiply,

$$
|\det M|=1\times14=14.
$$

Therefore

$$
28=14\times\operatorname{area}(ABC),
$$

so $\boxed{\operatorname{area}(ABC)=2\text{ cm}^2}$.

</details>

### 2024 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 1 · 5 marks

Let

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}k&1&0\\6&5&2\\-1&3&-k\end{pmatrix},
$$

where $k$ is real.

**(a)** Show that $A$ is non-singular. **[3]**

**(b)** Given that

$$
A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}3&0&-1\\1&0&0\\-\frac{23}{2}&\frac12&3\end{pmatrix},
$$

find $k$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Expanding along the first row,

$$
\det A
=k\begin{vmatrix}5&2\\3&-k\end{vmatrix}
-1\begin{vmatrix}6&2\\-1&-k\end{vmatrix}
=k(-5k-6)-(-6k+2)
=-5k^2-2.
$$

For real $k$, $-5k^2-2<0$, so $\det A\ne0$ and $A$ is non-singular.

**(b)** Use $AA^{-1}=I$. The top-left entry of the product is

$$
3k+1,
$$

which must equal $1$. Thus $3k+1=1$ and $\boxed{k=0}$.

</details>

### 2024 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 3 · 11 marks

Let

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}7&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** Give full details of the two transformations represented by $M$, in the correct order. **[4]**

**(b)** Find the invariant lines through the origin of the transformation represented by $M$. **[5]**

Triangle $DEF$ is transformed by $M$ onto triangle $PQR$ of area $35\text{ cm}^2$.

**(c)** Find the area of triangle $DEF$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Reading from right to left, first apply a one-way stretch parallel to the $x$-axis with scale factor $7$, then a shear with the $x$-axis fixed and $(0,1)$ mapped to $(2,1)$. Thus

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}7&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(b)** The image of $(x,mx)$ is

$$
\binom XY
=\begin{pmatrix}7&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\binom{x}{mx}
=\binom{(7+2m)x}{mx}.
$$

Requiring $Y=mX$ gives

$$
m=m(7+2m)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
2m^2+6m=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
2m(m+3)=0.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{y=0\quad\text{or}\quad y=-3x}.
$$

**(c)** The area factor is

$$
|\det M|=|7|=7.
$$

Thus $35=7\times\operatorname{area}(DEF)$ and

$$
\boxed{\operatorname{area}(DEF)=5\text{ cm}^2}.
$$

</details>

### 2024 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 1 · 10 marks

A stretch parallel to the $x$-axis with scale factor $k\ne0$ is followed by a shear with the $x$-axis fixed and $(0,1)$ mapped to $(k,1)$.

**(a)** Show that the combined matrix is $M=\begin{pmatrix}k&k\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. **[4]**

**(b)** The transformation has a line of invariant points. Find its equation. **[3]**

The unit square $S$ is transformed by $M$ onto parallelogram $P$.

**(c)** Find a matrix mapping $P$ back onto $S$. **[1]**

**(d)** Given that the area of $P$ is $3k^2$, find the possible values of $k$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** The stretch and shear matrices are, respectively,

$$
\begin{pmatrix}k&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}1&k\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The product in the stated order is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}1&k\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}k&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}k&k\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(b)** A point on the line of invariant points satisfies

$$
M\binom xy=\binom xy.
$$

Thus

$$
kx+ky=x,
$$

while the second coordinate is already unchanged. Since $k\ne0$,

$$
\boxed{y=\frac{1-k}{k}x}.
$$

**(c)** The required reverse transformation is represented by

$$
\boxed{M^{-1}=\frac1k\begin{pmatrix}1&-k\\0&k\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(d)** Since the unit square has area $1$, the area of $P$ is

$$
|\det M|=|k|.
$$

Hence

$$
|k|=3k^2.
$$

As $k\ne0$, division by $|k|$ gives $1=3|k|$, so

$$
\boxed{k=\pm\frac13}.
$$

</details>

### 2024 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 4 · 13 marks

Let

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&1&3\\3&2&5\end{pmatrix},\quad
B=\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\-1&3\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
C=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-1&1\\1&1&3\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** Show that $CAB=\begin{pmatrix}3&-7\\-9&3\end{pmatrix}$. **[3]**

**(b)** Find the invariant lines through the origin of the transformation represented by $CAB$. **[5]**

Let $M=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.

**(c)** Describe the transformation represented by $M$. **[2]**

**(d)** Find $N$ such that $NM=CAB$. **[3]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** First,

$$
AB
=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&1&3\\3&2&5\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\-1&3\\0&0\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-2&4\\-1&-1\\-2&0\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Therefore

$$
CAB
=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-1&1\\1&1&3\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}-2&4\\-1&-1\\-2&0\end{pmatrix}
=\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}3&-7\\-9&3\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(b)** For $y=mx$,

$$
\binom XY
=\binom{(3-7m)x}{(-9+3m)x}.
$$

The condition $Y=mX$ gives

$$
-9+3m=m(3-7m)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
7m^2=9.
$$

Thus

$$
\boxed{y=\frac3{\sqrt7}x\quad\text{or}\quad y=-\frac3{\sqrt7}x}.
$$

**(c)** $M$ is a one-way stretch parallel to the $x$-axis with scale factor $3$.

**(d)** Since $NM=CAB$,

$$
N=(CAB)M^{-1}
=\begin{pmatrix}3&-7\\-9&3\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1/3&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Therefore

$$
\boxed{N=\begin{pmatrix}1&-7\\-3&3\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

</details>

### 2025 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 4 · 9 marks

Let

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 0<\theta<2\pi.
$$

**(a)** State the two transformations represented by $M$, in the correct order. **[2]**

**(b)** Find the value of $\theta$ for which the transformation has a line of invariant points. **[7]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Reading the product from right to left, first rotate anticlockwise through $\theta$ about the origin, then apply a shear with the $x$-axis fixed and $(0,1)$ mapped to $(2,1)$.

**(b)** Multiplying gives

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta+2\sin\theta&2\cos\theta-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}.
$$

For a line of invariant points there must be a non-zero solution of

$$
M\binom xy=\binom xy.
$$

Equating coordinates gives

$$
(\cos\theta+2\sin\theta-1)x
+(2\cos\theta-\sin\theta)y=0,
$$

$$
\sin\theta\,x+(\cos\theta-1)y=0.
$$

These homogeneous equations have a non-zero solution only when the determinant of their coefficient matrix is zero:

$$
(\cos\theta+2\sin\theta-1)(\cos\theta-1)
-(2\cos\theta-\sin\theta)\sin\theta=0.
$$

Using $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$ simplifies this to

$$
\sin\theta+\cos\theta=1.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\sqrt2\sin\left(\theta+\frac\pi4\right)=1.
$$

In $0<\theta<2\pi$, the solutions of $\sin\theta+\cos\theta=1$ are $\theta=\pi/2$ and the excluded endpoint $\theta=0$ (equivalently $2\pi$). Therefore

$$
\boxed{\theta=\frac\pi2}.
$$

</details>

### 2025 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 1 · 11 marks

A one-way stretch parallel to the $x$-axis with scale factor $14$ is followed by a rotation anticlockwise about the origin through $\pi/3$. Let the combined matrix be $M$.

**(a)** Show that

$$
2M=\begin{pmatrix}14&-\sqrt3\\14\sqrt3&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**[4]**

**(b)** Find the invariant lines through the origin of the transformation represented by $M$. **[5]**

**(c)** Find $M^{-1}$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** The stretch and rotation matrices are

$$
\begin{pmatrix}14&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}\frac12&-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\[2pt]\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&\frac12\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Since the stretch is performed first,

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}\frac12&-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\[2pt]\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&\frac12\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}14&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}7&-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\[2pt]7\sqrt3&\frac12\end{pmatrix},
$$

and multiplying by $2$ proves the stated result.

**(b)** For a point $(x,mx)$,

$$
X=7x-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}mx,
\qquad
Y=7\sqrt3x+\frac12mx.
$$

The condition $Y=mX$ gives

$$
\sqrt3m^2-13m+14\sqrt3=0.
$$

The discriminant is $169-168=1$, so

$$
m=\frac{13\pm1}{2\sqrt3}
=2\sqrt3\quad\text{or}\quad\frac7{\sqrt3}.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{y=2\sqrt3x\quad\text{or}\quad y=\frac7{\sqrt3}x}.
$$

**(c)** Since $\det M=14$,

$$
M^{-1}
=\frac1{14}\begin{pmatrix}\frac12&\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\[2pt]-7\sqrt3&7\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\boxed{M^{-1}=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1/14&\sqrt3/14\\-\sqrt3&1\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

</details>

<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2025, Q1.</div>

### 2025 May/June · 9231/14 · Question 5 · 14 marks

A one-way stretch in the $x$-direction with scale factor $3$ is followed by reflection in $y=x$.

**(a)** Find the combined matrix $M$. **[3]**

**(b)** Give full details of the transformation represented by $M^{-1}$. **[3]**

Let $N$ satisfy $MN=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$.

**(c)** Find $N$. **[3]**

**(d)** Find the invariant lines through the origin of the transformation represented by $MN$. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** The stretch and reflection matrices are

$$
S=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
F=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The stretch is followed by the reflection, so

$$
\boxed{M=FS
=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\3&0\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(b)**

$$
M^{-1}=S^{-1}F^{-1}
=\begin{pmatrix}1/3&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/3\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Thus $M^{-1}$ represents reflection in $y=x$, followed by a one-way stretch parallel to the $x$-axis with scale factor $1/3$.

**(c)** Since $MN=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$,

$$
N=M^{-1}(MN)
=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/3\\1&0\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&2\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{N=M^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&2/3\\1&2\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(d)** For $y=mx$,

$$
\binom XY
=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&2\end{pmatrix}
\binom{x}{mx}
=\binom{(1+2m)x}{(3+2m)x}.
$$

The condition $Y=mX$ gives

$$
3+2m=m(1+2m)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
2m^2-m-3=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
(2m-3)(m+1)=0.
$$

Therefore

$$
\boxed{y=\frac32x\quad\text{or}\quad y=-x}.
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="matrices-2025-mj-14"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/14/M/J/2025, Q5.</div>

### 2025 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 2 · 11 marks

Let

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&\frac32\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\\frac32&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** Describe the transformation represented by $A$. **[2]**

**(b)** Describe the transformation represented by $B$. **[2]**

Triangle $DEF$ is transformed by $AB$ onto triangle $PQR$.

**(c)** Show that the two triangles have the same area. **[2]**

**(d)** Find the invariant lines through the origin of the transformation represented by $AB$. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** $A$ is a shear with the $x$-axis fixed and $(0,1)$ mapped to $(3/2,1)$.

**(b)** $B$ is a shear with the $y$-axis fixed and $(1,0)$ mapped to $(1,3/2)$.

**(c)** Multiplication gives

$$
AB=\begin{pmatrix}13/4&3/2\\3/2&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det(AB)=1,
$$

Therefore the area scale factor is $|\det(AB)|=1$, so the two triangles have the same area.

**(d)** For $y=mx$,

$$
\binom XY
=\begin{pmatrix}13/4&3/2\\3/2&1\end{pmatrix}
\binom{x}{mx}
=\binom{(13/4+3m/2)x}{(3/2+m)x}.
$$

The condition $Y=mX$ gives

$$
\frac32+m=m\left(\frac{13}{4}+\frac32m\right).
$$

After simplification,

$$
m^2+\frac32m-1=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
(m+2)\left(m-\frac12\right)=0.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{y=-2x\quad\text{or}\quad y=\frac12x}.
$$

</details>

### 2025 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 4 · 10 marks

Let $k,m$ be non-zero constants and

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
B=\begin{pmatrix}k&0\\0&m\end{pmatrix},\quad
C=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&1\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** Describe the transformation represented by $B$ when **(i)** $m=1$, and **(ii)** $m=k$. **[4]**

**(b)** Show that $ABC$ is singular. **[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)(i)** When $m=1$,

$$
B=\begin{pmatrix}k&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
$$

so $B$ represents a one-way stretch parallel to the $x$-axis with scale factor $k$.

**(a)(ii)** When $m=k$,

$$
B=\begin{pmatrix}k&0\\0&k\end{pmatrix}=kI,
$$

so $B$ represents an enlargement with centre the origin and scale factor $k$.

**(b)** First,

$$
AB
=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}k&0\\0&m\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}0&m\\-k&m\\k&m\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Therefore

$$
ABC=\begin{pmatrix}
m&m&2m\\
-2k+m&k+m&-k+2m\\
2k+m&-k+m&k+2m
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Expanding its determinant and collecting terms gives

$$
m(k+m)(k+2m)-m(-k+m)(-k+2m)-m(-2k+m)(k+2m)
$$

$$
{}+m(2k+m)(-k+2m)+2m(-2k+m)(-k+m)-2m(2k+m)(k+m)=0.
$$

The six expanded terms simplify to

$$
6m^2k+6m^2k-12m^2k=0.
$$

Hence $\det(ABC)=0$, so $ABC$ is singular.

</details>

::: {.question-card #matrices-2025-on-14}
### 2025 October/November · 9231/14 · Question 5 · 14 marks

**(a)** Show that

$$
\cos\frac\pi{12}=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4},\qquad
\sin\frac\pi{12}=\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}.
$$

**[2]**

Let

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\pi/12)&\sin(\pi/12)\\\sin(\pi/12)&-\cos(\pi/12)\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(b)** Give full details of the two transformations represented by $M$, in the correct order. **[4]**

**(c)** Write $M^{-1}$ as the product of two matrices, neither equal to $I$. **[2]**

**(d)** Given that $y=mx$ is invariant, show that

$$
m^2\sin\frac\pi{12}+2m\cos\frac\pi{12}-\sin\frac\pi{12}=0,
$$

and find $m$ in the requested cotangent/cosecant form. **[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Since $\pi/12=\pi/4-\pi/6$,

$$
\cos\frac\pi{12}
=\cos\frac\pi4\cos\frac\pi6
+\sin\frac\pi4\sin\frac\pi6
=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4},
$$

and

$$
\sin\frac\pi{12}
=\sin\frac\pi4\cos\frac\pi6
-\cos\frac\pi4\sin\frac\pi6
=\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}.
$$

**(b)** The matrix factorises as

$$
M=\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\pi/12)&-\sin(\pi/12)\\\sin(\pi/12)&\cos(\pi/12)\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Reading from right to left, first reflect in the $x$-axis, then rotate anticlockwise through $\pi/12$ about the origin.

**(c)** Reversing the order and inverting each factor gives

$$
\boxed{M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\pi/12)&\sin(\pi/12)\\-\sin(\pi/12)&\cos(\pi/12)\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(d)** Write $s=\sin(\pi/12)$ and $c=\cos(\pi/12)$. A point $(x,mx)$ maps to

$$
\binom XY=\binom{(c+ms)x}{(s-mc)x}.
$$

The condition $Y=mX$ gives

$$
s-mc=m(c+ms),
$$

so

$$
m^2s+2mc-s=0,
$$

as required. By the quadratic formula,

$$
m=\frac{-2c\pm\sqrt{4c^2+4s^2}}{2s}
=\frac{-c\pm1}{s}.
$$

Therefore

$$
\boxed{m=-\cot\frac\pi{12}\pm\cosec\frac\pi{12}}.
$$

</details>
